title: Model Predictive Adversarial Imitation Learning for Planning from Observation
claim: A planner is trained end-to-end by coupling a learned cost discriminator and a value function through shared transitions.
layout: 3 colored blocks, loop arrows between modules, planner on top, losses below
description: A block diagram with three rounded modules. The top gray box, 'Planning & Control', shows two robot icons and a bold black trajectory with dotted sampled rollouts. Green markers on the trajectory connect to a green trapezoid labeled C_theta (cost) on the left. Orange markers connect to an orange trapezoid labeled V_phi (value) on the right. A 'Transitions' line runs from the planner down to a double-headed arrow between the two lower boxes. The lower-left green 'Discriminator' box holds cylinders for Expert States and Generator States and a BCE loss box. The lower-right orange 'Value' box holds a Returns cylinder and a value loss box. Black feedback lines return from the losses to C_theta and V_phi. Green and orange color-code the cost and value pathways.
caption: Model Predictive Adversarial Imitation Learning (MPAIL) learns costs for a planning-based, Model Predictive Control (MPC) agent from observation-only demonstration. Interactions with these costs are simultaneously used to learn a value function for experience-based reasoning beyond the horizon of the planner.
abstract: Human demonstration data is often ambiguous and incomplete, motivating imitation learning approaches that also exhibit reliable planning behavior. A common paradigm to perform planning-from-demonstration involves learning a reward function via Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) then deploying this reward via Model Predictive Control (MPC). Towards unifying these methods, we derive a replacement of the policy in IRL with a planning-based agent. With connections to Adversarial Imitation Learning, this formulation enables end-to-end interactive learning of planners from observation-only demonstrations. In addition to benefits in interpretability, complexity, and safety, we study and observe significant improvements on sample efficiency, out-of-distribution generalization, and robustness. The study includes evaluations in both simulated control benchmarks and real-world navigation experiments using few-to-single observation-only demonstrations.
